opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot, and honestly I'm not sure "maintain" is quite the right word, because it implies more top-down steering than actually happens. The way I think about it is that there are a few big questions I care about: how language relates to the world, how we learn from language and not just about it, and what's actually going on inside models that seem to understand language. Those questions are broad enough that a lot of different projects can live under them.

When students come in, they usually have their own instincts. Some are more linguistically minded, some come from the machine learning side, some care about cognitive science or about building tools people actually use. I've found the most productive thing isn't to assign a project from some master plan. It's to find where what they're excited about intersects with those core questions. Often the student ends up pulling the lab in a direction I wouldn't have predicted, and that's a feature, not a bug.

The coherence comes less from a fixed agenda and more from a shared set of tastes, a sense of what makes a question interesting. Even if one person works on interpretability, another on grounded language learning, and another on using language as supervision for policies or programs, there's a common thread: language is a lens, both for building systems that learn more efficiently and for understanding what those systems are doing. Lab meetings and informal conversations help a lot. People see connections between their projects that I didn't plan, and collaborations form organically.

There's also some natural evolution over time. The things we worked on five or six years ago look different from what we work on now, partly because the field changed dramatically with large language models, and partly because students brought in new perspectives. So I'd say the direction is coherent in the way a conversation is coherent, not in the way a blueprint is. It holds together because people keep responding to each other, not because I've drawn the whole map in advance.

r001.rationale: The response says students’ interests can pull the lab in unexpected directions, but does not describe a shift from Jacob Andreas’s prepared project list to projects sourced elsewhere.

r002.rationale: It says lab meetings and informal conversations help members see connections across projects and form collaborations, keeping the direction coherent through people responding to one another.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, and honestly I'm not sure I'd describe what happens in my lab as maintaining a coherent direction so much as discovering one after the fact.

When I started the group, I had a fairly specific picture in my head: I wanted to understand how language can be used to structure learning. How you can take the compositional structure of language and use it to build models that generalize in more human-like ways. And some of the early work really did look like that. But the thing you learn very quickly as an advisor is that the students who are going to do the best work are the ones who come in with their own obsessions, and those obsessions are never exactly yours.

So I've ended up thinking about it less as a direction and more as a set of questions that I personally find interesting enough that I'm happy to keep coming back to them, and that are broad enough that a lot of different projects can be in conversation with them. Something like: what do these models actually know, how is that knowledge represented, and how can we communicate with them, in both directions, using language? A student who wants to do interpretability work on transformers fits into that. A student who wants to think about how a robot should learn from instructions fits into that. A student who's interested in cognitive science and how children acquire word meanings fits into that too, even though those three people might not initially see themselves as working on the same thing.

The practical mechanism, I think, is just that we talk a lot. Group meetings matter, but so does the fact that when someone brings me a problem I'll try to connect it to something another student is doing. Over time the students start making those connections themselves, and you end up with this web of shared vocabulary and shared tools that holds the group together even when the surface-level topics look quite different.

And then there's a part of this that's just me being honest about my own limitations. My research interests have drifted over the years partly because my students pulled me in directions I wouldn't have gone on my own. When language models got good, a lot of the questions I'd been thinking about in a fairly narrow setting suddenly became much more interesting at scale, and that shift happened in large part because students were excited about it before I was. So I'd say the coherence isn't something I impose. It's more like a center of gravity that moves as the people in the group change, and my job is mostly to keep asking whether the things we're doing still speak to each other.

r001.rationale: The candidate says students bring their own interests and pull the lab in new directions, but it does not describe a shift from Jacob’s prepared project list to projects sourced elsewhere.

r002.rationale: The candidate identifies frequent conversation, including connecting one student’s problem to another’s work, as how students build shared connections that hold the group together.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as an ongoing conversation. Students arrive with interests of their own, and those interests evolve as they discover what they’re good at and what problems they find compelling. My job isn’t to make sure everybody keeps working on exactly the question I had in mind when they joined. It’s to help them develop those interests into a research agenda, while finding connections to the questions the rest of us are thinking about.

There’s a useful tension there. You want enough shared intellectual ground that people can give each other meaningful feedback, but enough independence that they can surprise you. Coherence doesn’t have to mean that all the projects look alike. It can come from a set of questions that people keep returning to, or from a shared way of approaching problems.

And that direction should change. If students are becoming independent researchers, then they should be influencing what I’m interested in, too. The lab’s agenda is something we develop together, rather than something I set once and then ask everyone to follow.

r001.rationale: The response says students’ interests shape a shared, evolving agenda, but does not describe a shift from Jacob Andreas’s prepared project list to most projects coming from elsewhere.

r002.rationale: It describes an ongoing conversation in which lab members give each other meaningful feedback, linking that exchange and shared intellectual ground to the lab’s coherence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as a process that goes in both directions. Students come in with their own interests, and those interests evolve as they discover what they’re excited about. Part of my job is to help them turn that excitement into a research question that we can actually make progress on. But that also changes what I’m interested in and what the lab works on.

So the coherence doesn’t necessarily come from everybody working toward a single predefined goal. It comes from having shared questions and ways of thinking about problems, and then talking to each other a lot. You want enough overlap that people can give each other useful feedback, but enough independence that a student can take the research somewhere you wouldn’t have thought to take it yourself.

r001.rationale: The response says students’ interests evolve and affect the lab, but does not describe a shift away from Jacob’s prepared project list toward projects from elsewhere.

r002.rationale: It says coherence comes from shared questions and ways of thinking, along with lab members “talking to each other a lot” so they can give one another useful feedback.
